When Past Experiences Continue to Affect How Safe You Feel Today

Perhaps an event, or a series of experiences over time, has left your mind and body feeling constantly on guard, even when you are in a safe environment today.

Maybe certain places, sounds, conversations, or anniversaries bring sudden waves of distress, tension, or overwhelm. Or perhaps you find yourself feeling emotionally detached, exhausted from staying hyper-alert, or working hard to avoid anything that reminds you of the past.

You may have told yourself that "it happened a long time ago", "others had it worse", or "you should be over it by now", only to feel frustrated when logic alone does not settle your nervous system.

Trauma is not defined solely by what happened, but by how an overwhelming experience continues to shape your nervous system, sense of safety, beliefs, and everyday relationships.

If these experiences feel familiar, you do not have to navigate them on your own.

With paced, trauma-informed support, it is possible to build greater present-day steadiness and work through the impact of past experiences at a rhythm that feels safe for you.

Could This Be What You're Experiencing?

Responses to trauma vary widely from person to person. Some adults experience vivid memories or heightened alertness, while others notice quiet patterns of emotional numbness, self-doubt, or difficulty trusting others.

You may notice that you:

  • feel constantly on edge, easily startled, or hyper-aware of your surroundings
  • experience unwanted memories, distressing dreams, or sudden emotional reactions to reminders
  • avoid certain places, conversations, people, or feelings that bring up discomfort
  • feel emotionally numb, disconnected from yourself, or detached from people you care about
  • struggle with disrupted sleep, difficulty concentrating, or persistent physical tension
  • carry strong feelings of guilt, shame, self-blame, or feeling fundamentally unsafe
  • notice sudden shifts in mood, irritability, or overwhelm during everyday stress
  • find it difficult to trust others, set boundaries, or feel at ease in close relationships

Experiencing these signs does not automatically mean you have a specific diagnosis such as PTSD. Similar responses can arise following single incidents, prolonged relationship or childhood stress, medical events, workplace incidents, or grief.

A supportive, clinically informed consultation can help clarify what may be contributing to how you are feeling and what type of care may be appropriate.

You May Be Looking for Support Because...

Every adult reaches out for trauma-informed support at a different point.

You may be seeking help because:

  • past experiences continue to affect your sleep, mood, confidence, or daily routines
  • you feel exhausted from staying on high alert or pushing difficult feelings away
  • triggers or strong emotional reactions are affecting your work or close relationships
  • you are navigating the impact of recent or long-standing relational, developmental, or workplace trauma
  • you want a safe, respectful therapeutic space where you will not be rushed into sharing more than you are ready for
  • you have spoken with your GP about a Mental Health Treatment Plan and want to find an appropriately trained practitioner

You do not need to have everything worked out, or be ready to tell your whole story, before reaching out.

Understanding Trauma

How the Nervous System Protects After Overwhelming Experiences

When you go through an experience that overwhelms your capacity to cope in the moment, your brain and nervous system automatically shift into survival mode, mobilising fight, flight, or freeze responses to protect you.

Sometimes, even after the danger or distressing situation has passed, the nervous system continues to operate as if the threat is still present. Everyday reminders can activate intense physical or emotional reactions before your thinking mind has time to evaluate the situation.

This is a protective stress response, not a sign of personal weakness.

Trauma-informed therapy recognises how deeply safety, pacing, and choice matter, focusing first on present-day grounding and stability before exploring difficult memories at a pace you control.

When Trauma Affects Everyday Life

Unresolved trauma can influence several areas of adult functioning at once.

Sense of Safety and Hypervigilance

Feeling persistently watchful, tense, or braced for something to go wrong can make genuine rest and relaxation feel unfamiliar.

Emotional Regulation

You may experience sudden surges of anxiety, anger, sadness, or shame, or swing toward feeling shut down, foggy, or disconnected.

Sleep and Physical Wellbeing

Difficulty falling asleep, restless nights, fatigue, muscle tension, and stress-related physical discomfort are common ways the body holds prolonged strain.

Focus and Everyday Routines

When significant energy goes into managing internal distress or avoiding triggers, concentration, memory, and daily decision-making can feel harder.

Self-Beliefs and Identity

Difficult experiences can leave lingering beliefs, such as "I am not safe", "It was my fault", or "I cannot trust anyone", that quietly shape daily choices.

Everyone's response to trauma is individual, and support is always tailored around your readiness and personal boundaries.

When Trauma Affects Relationships

How Past Experiences Ripple Into Connection

Because trust, vulnerability, and emotional safety are central to close relationships, the impact of trauma often shows up alongside partners, family members, or colleagues.

You might find yourself pulling back to feel protected, struggling to explain why certain situations feel overwhelming, or feeling misunderstood by people around you.

Over time, this can contribute to:

  • difficulty feeling fully present, relaxed, or emotionally open with loved ones
  • avoiding conflict, closeness, or conversations that feel emotionally risky
  • feeling easily overwhelmed, defensive, or misunderstood during disagreements
  • patterns of people-pleasing or difficulty stating personal boundaries
  • feeling isolated even within supportive relationships

Recognising these patterns is not about blame: it provides a compassionate starting point for building safer, clearer connections.

You Don't Have to Figure It Out Alone

Safe, Paced, Evidence-Based Support Tailored to You

Trauma-informed therapy is built on collaboration, transparency, and respect for your pace. You remain in control of what you share and when you explore deeper material.

Depending on your individual needs and goals, therapy may focus on:

  • establishing emotional safety, grounding skills, and nervous system stabilisation first
  • understanding how trauma responses and triggers operate in everyday life
  • building practical tools to manage overwhelm, sleep disruption, and emotional shifts
  • gently processing distressing memories using evidence-based approaches when you feel ready
  • exploring unhelpful self-beliefs around safety, responsibility, and self-worth
  • strengthening boundaries, self-trust, and communication in relationships

Support moves at a pace that prioritises your stability and wellbeing at every stage.

What Could Change with the Right Support?

With tailored, trauma-informed psychological support, many adults gradually experience greater steadiness and connection in everyday life.

Depending on your individual goals and circumstances, therapy may help you:

  • feel more grounded and settled in your body during day-to-day routines
  • recognise triggers earlier and use practical calming strategies when distress rises
  • reduce the intensity or frequency of intrusive memories and avoidance patterns
  • support steadier sleep habits and everyday energy
  • approach relationships and boundaries with greater clarity and self-trust
  • relate to yourself with greater compassion rather than self-blame

Progress is individualised and rarely linear, and a steady, respectful therapeutic relationship provides consistent support along the way.

Small Changes Can Make Everyday Life More Manageable

Practical Grounding Steps Alongside Therapy

When your nervous system feels stretched, gentle present-moment anchors can help remind your body that you are safe right now.

Alongside professional support, many adults find it helpful to:

  • use sensory grounding techniques, such as noticing five things you can see, feeling your feet on the floor, or holding a warm mug, when distress rises
  • practise slow, extended exhales to signal safety to your nervous system
  • maintain predictable daily anchors around waking, meals, movement, and winding down for sleep
  • give yourself permission to pause and step away from overwhelming conversations or media
  • create a calm, comfortable space at home where you can decompress without demands
  • treat difficult reactions with curiosity rather than criticism, reminding yourself that your nervous system is trying to protect you

Strategies work best when adapted to your comfort level, daily routines, and personal preferences.

What Could Support Look Like?

Individualised Care for Adults

Because trauma affects individuals differently, care is tailored around your history, preferences, and clinical needs.

Trauma-Informed Psychological Therapy

Depending on your practitioner's training and your goals, evidence-based approaches, such as Trauma-Focused Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (TF-CBT), Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing (EMDR), Schema Therapy, Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), or phased somatic and relational approaches, may help support stabilisation and recovery.

Stabilisation and Coping Skills Support

Early sessions often focus on practical grounding, emotional regulation, and daily routine support so you feel well-resourced throughout therapy.

GP and Medical Support

If trauma-related stress is affecting your sleep, mood, or physical health, your General Practitioner (GP) can discuss a Mental Health Treatment Plan where eligible and explore whether medical review or broader healthcare support may be appropriate alongside psychological care.

You Don't Need to Know Where to Start

Taking the First Step at Your Own Pace

Reaching out for trauma support can feel daunting, especially if you are unsure which therapy style is suitable or feel anxious about explaining what you have been through.

You do not need to share sensitive details during your initial enquiry, nor do you need to have everything figured out before contacting us.

At Michelle Barratt Psychology, our team listens respectfully to what you feel comfortable sharing, explains available pathways clearly, and helps match you with an appropriately trained practitioner.

Whether you are:

  • exploring trauma-informed support for the first time
  • seeking a practitioner trained in approaches such as EMDR or trauma-focused therapy
  • holding a GP Mental Health Treatment Plan and looking for a supportive fit
  • wanting in-person sessions in Brisbane or private online appointments from home

we are here to help make taking that first step feel safe, respectful, and manageable.

Why Clients Choose MBP

Clinically Informed Support, With You at the Centre

Michelle Barratt Psychology & Administration Services (MBP) provides a welcoming, neutral, and professionally managed entry point for adults seeking psychological and allied health care.

Clinically Informed Intake

Sensitive, respectful intake processes help us understand your preferences and identify a suitable support pathway.

Appropriate Practitioner Matching

We connect you with clinical psychologists, general psychologists, social workers, or counsellors whose experience and scope of practice align with trauma-informed care.

Coordinated Care

Where appropriate and with your consent, practitioners can liaise with your GP and other health professionals involved in your care.

Practical Referral Support

Our team assists with GP referral requirements, Mental Health Treatment Plans, and Medicare-related paperwork where applicable.

Flexible Access

In-person appointments are available at our Brisbane clinics in Toowong and Manly West, alongside secure Online Therapy / Telehealth Australia-wide where clinically appropriate.

Start with a Conversation

You Don't Have to Carry the Weight of the Past Alone

You may not be sure which therapy approach is right for you, or how to begin talking about what you have experienced.

If past events continue to make everyday life feel harder than it should and you would like steady, non-judgmental support, reaching out can be a helpful first step.

Share only as much as feels comfortable, and our team will help you explore an appropriate pathway forward.

Contact Michelle Barratt Psychology on (07) 3185 0040 or reach out via our online contact form to learn more about individual and adult trauma therapy support.
